description: We are building one consistent fire calendar for Nepal, usable anywhere on Earth. We harmonize 25 years of NASA MODIS hotspots with the sharper VIIRS record so the sensor no longer matters, then show which months and years burn most, how this month compares with the historical median, and a CSV of every hotspot. The Kathmandu Valley breathes smoke every spring. Looking for: data analysis, web development, design and Earth science.
summary: Agni gives Nepal one consistent record of fire activity from 2000 to today, built from NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots. NASA's two fire sensors see Nepal very differently: in 2021, MODIS recorded 7,631 vegetation-fire hotspots and VIIRS recorded 56,374, so the two records cannot be compared or joined, and MODIS is nearing the end of its life. Agni merges VIIRS detections into MODIS-sized 1 km cells per day and converts them to MODIS-equivalent counts with one factor per calendar month, fitted on 2012–2019 only. On 2020–2024, years the fit never used, Agni's monthly counts differ from MODIS by a median of 15%, against 500% for raw VIIRS and 25% for a single fixed ratio. The web app shows a month-by-year fire calendar for Nepal, any province or district, or any area drawn on the map; the normal fire year for that area; this week compared with the 25-year median; and CSV downloads. It also shows that Nepal's spring fires are rising by about 930 hotspots per decade. Forest officers already get alerts about where fires are burning; Agni tells them whether a season is unusual.
details:
• Live app: https://agni-fire-calendar.vercel.app

• 30-second demo: https://youtu.be/AhN0RhjQCss

• Slides: https://agni-fire-calendar.vercel.app/deck.pdf

• Code and method: https://github.com/shuv-amp/nasa-space-challenge

WHAT IT DOES

Agni gives Nepal one consistent record of fire activity from 2000 to today, built from NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots. Two NASA sensors have watched Nepal's fires: MODIS since 2000 and VIIRS since 2012. They see fire very differently. In 2021, MODIS recorded 7,631 vegetation-fire hotspots in Nepal and VIIRS recorded 56,374. Joined naively, the record jumps in 2012 for reasons that have nothing to do with fire, and MODIS is close to the end of its life. Agni converts VIIRS into MODIS-equivalent counts, so the sensor no longer matters and the record can continue after MODIS stops.

The web app shows:

• A month-by-year burning calendar (2000–2025) for all of Nepal, any of its 7 provinces or 75 districts, or any box drawn on the map. You can switch between the harmonized record, MODIS only and raw VIIRS to see why harmonization is needed.

• What a normal fire year looks like for the chosen area: the 25-year median for each month and the range that counts as unusual (for Nepal, a normal April has about 1,272 hotspots; above about 2,968 is a top-10% April).

• This week compared with the same week in every year since 2001, from FIRMS near-real-time data (9–15 Nov 2026: 15 MODIS hotspots against a median of 9).

• A day-by-day replay of the 2021 spring season as MODIS, VIIRS and Agni each count it.

• CSV downloads of every hotspot in the selected area and of the monthly harmonized series.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: FIRMS yearly files for Nepal, MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra and Aqua, 1 km) and VIIRS S-NPP 375 m, plus the FIRMS 7-day near-real-time feed.

2. Cleaning: vegetation fires only (MODIS confidence 30 or more, VIIRS nominal or high confidence, static and offshore sources removed). This leaves 74,133 MODIS and 387,447 VIIRS detections.

3. Matching footprints: VIIRS pixels are about nine times smaller in area than MODIS pixels, so one fire often lights up several neighbouring VIIRS pixels. We merge VIIRS detections into roughly 1 km cells per day and per day/night pass, which turns 387,447 detections into 278,070 cells.

4. Calibration: one factor for each calendar month converts VIIRS cells into MODIS-equivalent counts. The factors are fitted on 2012–2019 only and range from 0.16 in March–April (large fires both sensors see) to 0.26 in December (small burns VIIRS catches more often). Months with few fires are pulled toward the overall ratio so they can't swing wildly.

5. Series: The calendar uses MODIS before 2012 and calibrated VIIRS from 2012 onward.

HOW WELL IT WORKS

We checked the method on 2020–2024, five years that were not used for fitting, by comparing Agni's monthly counts for Nepal with the MODIS counts:


• Agni: median error 15%, total difference −5.4% over 58 months, R² 0.976 on log counts.

• Raw VIIRS: median error 500%, total difference +663%.

• A single fixed ratio for all months: median error 25%.

At a finer scale (1° areas, month by month) Agni's median error is 23% against 673% for raw VIIRS. We also tried separate factors for each province. They did not help (24% vs 23%), so one national set is used, and the remaining local error appears to come mostly from small monthly counts.

WHAT WE FOUND

• Nepal burns mostly in spring: about 87% of hotspots fall in February–May, and April alone holds about half. The worst years were 2021, 2016 and 2024.

• Spring fire activity is rising: about 930 more MODIS hotspots per decade between 2001 and 2025 (Mann–Kendall p = 0.02). We used MODIS alone for this, so no sensor change is involved. The timing of the season (its start, middle and end) shows no significant trend: more fire, not an earlier season.

• The fire is concentrated in the west and the Terai: Bardiya, Surkhet, Kailali, Chitawan and Dang have the most hotspots. Bhaktapur district, where our event is held, has had only 2 in 25 years, so the smoke the Kathmandu Valley breathes each spring comes from fires elsewhere.

WHO IT IS FOR AND WHY IT MATTERS

Nepal's Department of Forests and Soil Conservation already receives satellite fire alerts through a system built with ICIMOD's SERVIR-HKH programme, using MODIS and VIIRS. An alert says where a fire is burning. It does not say whether this week, this month or this district is unusual, and its two sensors count fires on different scales. Agni supplies that context: one consistent 25-year baseline and a normal range for every district and month. Division forest offices can plan for their real peak, early-warning and air-quality teams can see when activity is above normal, and district offices can download their own data for reports.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib) for downloading, cleaning, gridding, calibration and testing; JavaScript and D3 for the web app; Canvas for the fire animations; geoBoundaries for province and district borders; Vercel for hosting; Playwright for testing in Chrome, Safari and Firefox. All fire data comes from NASA FIRMS.

WHAT IS NEW ABOUT IT

Instead of comparing raw counts or applying one fixed ratio, Agni first puts both sensors into the same unit (1 km cell-days) and then lets the conversion change with the season. It is tested on years it never saw and the error is shown on the page next to the simple alternatives. The result is a calendar that anyone can read, not a model only specialists can use.


LIMITS WE CONSIDERED

• A hotspot is a heat detection at the moment a satellite passes over, not burned area. Small, short or understory fires are missed.

• Clouds and thick smoke hide fires from both sensors, most at the spring peak. In spring 2021 Agni's total was 12% below MODIS.

• The calibration is fitted for Nepal. Other countries should refit the factors with the same code. Land cover may change them, which we have not yet tested.

• The yearly record ends in December 2025. The current week uses MODIS near-real-time data only.

• MODIS will retire. Agni is anchored on the years when both sensors overlap, so the record can continue on VIIRS alone, and the same method can add the newer VIIRS satellites (NOAA-20 and NOAA-21).
